implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types, not authorization: the guard is a higher-order function whose signature ties the policy to the request context, and the policy is a module of pure functions returning a discriminated decision ({ allowed: true } | { allowed: false; reason: string }) so denial handling is exhaustively typed. Middleware composition and route registration are the enforcement point, and the request-scoped subject travels on the request object or in an AsyncLocalStorage store. What replaces the classic structure: functions returning functions replace the Guard class and narrowing keeps the decision types exact without class hierarchies; choose the NestJS variant when the application already uses that framework's DI and decorators.
idiom_name: higher-order middleware guard + discriminated decision type
pitfalls: Route registration order is the enforcement contract; a handler registered without the guard is unprotected - consider a global guard and explicit public routes.
A non-null assertion (req.securityContext!) hides a missing context; model it as optional and deny when absent, as the sketch does.
Types vanish at run time: a Policy-shaped value loaded from configuration is unvalidated input, and no type annotation enforces a rule.

variants.name: NestJS CanActivate guard + @UseGuards metadata
variants.implementation_notes: In NestJS the guard is a first-class framework construct: a class implementing CanActivate with canActivate(context: ExecutionContext) returning boolean/Promise/Observable, applied with @UseGuards at controller, method or global scope, with rule data attached through @SetMetadata / Reflector.createDecorator and read back via Reflector (docs.nestjs.com/guards). The policy is whatever the guard consults - a DI-injected service, a rules object or an external PDP - and the framework throws ForbiddenException when canActivate returns false. What replaces the classic structure: the execution context, metadata reflection and DI-instantiated guard class replace a hand-written wrapper and per-method rule registration; use this variant only inside a Nest application.
pitfalls: `if (!roles) return true` fails open for every undecorated handler; when metadata is missing, decide the default deliberately (usually deny).
Global guards created with useGlobalGuards(new X()) outside a module cannot inject dependencies; register through the APP_GUARD token so the policy service is injected.
Guards run after middleware and before interceptors/pipes, so they see the raw request only - parse and validate there rather than expecting transformed data.
variants.idiom_name: CanActivate guard class with Reflector metadata (@UseGuards)
